content: The World Health Organization (WHO) issued guidelines in November 2017 addressing the use of medically important antimicrobials in food-producing animals. The overuse and misuse of antibiotics in both humans and animals are major contributors to the growing threat of antibiotic resistance. Some bacteria responsible for severe human infections have already developed resistance to most or all available treatments, with few promising alternatives in development. If no action is taken, it is projected that by 2050, nearly all current antibiotics will become ineffective, leading to a global economic loss exceeding $100 trillion due to reduced productivity. This highlights the urgency of the WHO’s 2011 slogan on antimicrobial resistance: “No action today, no cure tomorrow.” Scientific evidence demonstrates that the overuse of antibiotics in animals contributes to the emergence of antibiotic resistance. The WHO guidelines build on decades of expert evaluations regarding the role of agricultural antibiotic use in driving resistance. These guidelines are a direct response to the Global Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance adopted by the 68th World Health Assembly in 2015 and the political declaration from the United Nations General Assembly in 2016. Both documents emphasize the global nature of antibiotic resistance and the rapid spread of resistant organisms and resistance genes across continents. They also recognize that all uses of antibiotics, whether in humans or animals, contribute to the development of resistance. The WHO guidelines aim to protect the effectiveness of antibiotics critical for human medicine by reducing their unnecessary use in animals. They are based on robust scientific evidence and are designed to be applicable across all countries, regardless of income level or scale of food animal production. The recommendations address the use of antibiotics in animals for growth promotion, disease prevention in the absence of disease, and the treatment and control of diagnosed diseases. The guidelines utilize the WHO’s list of critically important antimicrobials for human medicine, which categorizes antibiotics into three groups—“important,” “highly important,” and “critically important”—based on their significance to human health. Key recommendations include: 1. A general reduction in the use of all medically important antimicrobials in food-producing animals. 2. A complete ban on the use of medically important antimicrobials for growth promotion in animals. 3. Avoiding the use of critically important antimicrobials for controlling the spread of clinically diagnosed infectious diseases within groups of animals. 4. Restricting the use of highest-priority critically important antimicrobials for treating food-producing animals with diagnosed infections, unless no other treatment options are available and only under the guidance of a qualified veterinarian. The guidelines also include best practice statements, such as ensuring that any new class of antibiotics developed for human use is automatically considered critically important unless otherwise specified by WHO. Additionally, medically important antimicrobials not currently used in food production should not be introduced for such purposes in the future. The recommendations were developed by a Guideline Development Group (GDG) comprising 13 external experts from diverse fields, including human and veterinary medicine, microbiology, antimicrobial resistance, agricultural economics, and veterinary ethics. The guidelines also align with the “One Health” approach, which addresses health risks at the intersection of human, animal, and environmental health. Implementing these guidelines may require significant changes in current practices in food animal production. Alternatives to antibiotics, such as improved hygiene, enhanced biosecurity, and better use of vaccines, have proven effective in maintaining productivity and animal health without relying on antibiotics for growth promotion or disease prevention. Countries that have already banned antimicrobial growth promoters can share their experiences to support implementation in other regions, particularly in developing countries. The WHO encourages countries to establish national surveillance programs to monitor antibiotic use in agriculture and the presence of antibiotic resistance in food animals, food products, humans, and the environment. This data will help evaluate the impact of implementing the guidelines. WHO will review and update these recommendations five years after publication, or sooner if significant new evidence emerges.
